items.question_text: A 2 kg box and a 4 kg box are both lifted from the floor onto the same table. Compare the increase in the energy in their gravitational potential energy stores.

options.a: It is the same for both boxes
options.b: It is twice as much for the 4 kg box
options.c: It is half as much for the 4 kg box
options.d: It is four times as much for the 4 kg box

feedback.b: The boxes are lifted through the same height, so they gain the same energy.
feedback.c: The heavier box does not gain less energy: both rise the same height.
feedback.d: Energy does not depend on the square of the mass.

misconception_map.b: slip: thinks more mass means more energy stored
misconception_map.c: slip: inverted the relationship with mass

items.explanation: Both boxes rise through the same height, so the increase in their gravitational potential energy stores is the same.

items.question_text: A crane lifts a steel beam 12 m vertically. The energy in the beam's gravitational potential energy store increases by \(58\,800\,\text{J}\). Gravitational field strength, \(g = 9.8\,\text{N/kg}\). Calculate the mass of the beam.

wrong.misconception: This leaves out \(g\). Rearrange \(E_p = mgh\) to \(m = \dfrac{E_p}{gh} = \dfrac{58\,800}{9.8 \times 12} = 500\,\text{kg}\).
This divides the wrong way round. \(m = \dfrac{E_p}{gh} = \dfrac{58\,800}{117.6} = 500\,\text{kg}\).

items.question_text: A satellite is lifted to an orbit 400 km above the Earth's surface. Why would using g = 9.8 N/kg in the gravitational potential energy equation give the wrong value for the energy needed?

options.a: The gravitational field strength is smaller at that height
options.b: The satellite has no mass once it is in orbit
options.c: The equation only works for objects touching the ground
options.d: The height is too small compared with the Earth to matter

feedback.b: The satellite's mass does not change in orbit.
feedback.c: The equation applies to changes in height above the ground as well.
feedback.d: 400 km is large enough for g to change noticeably.

misconception_map.b: slip: thinks objects in orbit have no mass
misconception_map.c: slip: thinks the equation only applies at ground level

items.explanation: g decreases with distance from the Earth's centre. At 400 km it is about 8.7 N/kg, so using 9.8 N/kg for the whole height overestimates the energy.

items.question_text: A hiker has a weight of 600 N. She walks 4 km along a winding mountain path and rises 300 m vertically. Gravitational field strength, \(g = 9.8\,\text{N/kg}\). How much energy is transferred to her gravitational potential energy store?

feedback.a: This finds her mass (600 ÷ 9.8) but then leaves out \(g\). Since weight \(= mg\), energy gained \(= mgh = \text{weight} \times h = 600 \times 300 = 180\,000\,\text{J}\).
feedback.c: This uses 600 as the mass. 600 N is her weight, which already includes \(g\): energy gained \(= \text{weight} \times h = 600 \times 300 = 180\,000\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: This uses the 4 km along the path. Only the vertical height gained counts: \(600 \times 300 = 180\,000\,\text{J}\).

misconception_map.a: slip: converted the weight to a mass and then left out g

items.explanation: Weight \(= mg\), so \(E_p = mgh = \text{weight} \times h = 600 \times 300 = 180\,000\,\text{J}\). The distance along the path is not needed, and \(g\) is already included in the weight.

items.question_text: A box is lifted onto a shelf. Which change would increase the energy transferred to its gravitational potential energy store?

options.b: Lifting it onto a higher shelf
options.c: Using a longer ramp to reach the same shelf
options.d: Painting the box a lighter colour

feedback.a: Lifting more slowly changes the power, not the energy stored.
feedback.c: Only the vertical height gained matters, not the length of the ramp.
feedback.d: The colour of the box has no effect on the energy stored.

misconception_map.d: slip: thinks colour affects the energy stored

items.explanation: Ep = mass × g × height gained, so only a greater mass, or a greater vertical height, increases it.

items.stem: A [[who]] of mass \([[m]]\,\text{kg}\) climbs some stairs. The energy in their gravitational potential energy store increases by \([[E]]\,\text{J}\). Gravitational field strength, \(g = [[g]]\,\text{N/kg}\). Calculate the vertical height they climb.

feedback.no-g: This leaves out \(g\). Rearrange \(E_p = mgh\) to \(h = \dfrac{E_p}{mg} = \dfrac{[[E]]}{[[m]] \times [[g]]}\).
feedback.upside-down: This divides the wrong way round. \(h = \dfrac{E_p}{mg}\): the energy goes on top.

items.stem: A [[thing]] of mass \([[m]]\,\text{kg}\) is lifted \([[h]]\,\text{m}\) vertically onto a shelf. Gravitational field strength, \(g = [[g]]\,\text{N/kg}\). Calculate the increase in the energy in its gravitational potential energy store.

misconception_map.divided-height: slip: divided by the height instead of multiplying

feedback.no-g: This leaves out \(g\). Multiply mass, \(g\) and height: \([[m]] \times [[g]] \times [[h]]\).
feedback.divided-height: This divides by the height. Multiply all three: \(E_p = mgh = [[m]] \times [[g]] \times [[h]]\).

This divides by the height. Multiply all three: \(E_p = mgh = 14 \times 9.8 \times 1.2\).

items.question_text: Two identical boxes of mangoes are raised from the ground onto the same lorry. Box X is lifted straight up. Box Y is pushed up a long, sloping ramp. Compare the increase in the energy in their gravitational potential energy stores.

options.a: It is the same for both boxes
options.b: It is greater for box Y, because it moves further
options.c: It is greater for box X, because it rises more steeply
options.d: It depends on how quickly each box is raised

feedback.b: The distance along the ramp does not matter. The gravitational store depends on the vertical height gained, which is the same for both boxes.
feedback.c: Steepness does not matter. Both boxes gain the same vertical height, so their gravitational stores increase by the same amount.
feedback.d: The time taken changes the power, not the energy. Both boxes gain the same vertical height, so the same energy is stored.

misconception_map.c: slip: thinks a steeper path stores more energy
misconception_map.d: slip: confuses the energy stored with the rate of transfer

items.explanation: Energy in the gravitational potential energy store depends on mass, g and the vertical height gained (Ep = mgh). The boxes are identical and end at the same height, so the increase is the same, whatever path they take.

items.question_text: A cyclist of mass 50 kg rides 120 m up a hill road. The road rises 6 m vertically. Gravitational field strength, \(g = 9.8\,\text{N/kg}\). How much energy is transferred to the cyclist's gravitational potential energy store?

feedback.a: This divides by the height. Multiply mass, \(g\) and height: \(50 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 2940\,\text{J}\).
feedback.b: This leaves out \(g\). Energy in the gravitational store \(= mgh = 50 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 2940\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: This uses the 120 m along the road. Only the vertical height gained counts: \(50 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 2940\,\text{J}\).

misconception_map.a: slip: divided by the height instead of multiplying

items.explanation: Only the vertical height gained matters, not the distance along the road. Gravitational potential energy gained \(= mgh = 50 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 2940\,\text{J}\).
